strengths: The paper tackles an important active perception problem and gives a clean POMDP-style formulation that unifies prediction and action selection through a supervised loss plus RL objective.

APPLE is evaluated on several tasks spanning classification and regression, including tactile MNIST classification, volume estimation, and wrench pose estimation, with 5 seeds and learning curves rather than only final numbers.
The random-policy baseline is useful and shows that learned exploration matters on several tasks, especially CircleSquare, TactileMNIST, and Toolbox.
The empirical results suggest that off-policy variants, especially APPLE-CrossQ, can be substantially more sample-efficient and robust than the HAM/REINFORCE-style baseline in these settings.
The paper includes implementation details, hyperparameters, hardware notes, limitations, and a stated intention to release code, which helps reproducibility.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate: the core method is largely an adaptation of standard off-policy actor-critic algorithms with a prediction-loss reward and transformer history encoder. The paper does not clearly separate what is algorithmically new from sensible engineering choices.

The central claim of general active perception is stronger than the evidence. Most experiments are simulated tactile or toy tasks from a closely related benchmark family; there is no real-robot experiment, multimodal setting, transfer experiment, or substantially different active perception domain.

Baselines are limited. HAM is an older on-policy method and in several tasks is either not applicable or performs poorly; comparisons to stronger active perception methods, information-gain/uncertainty heuristics, model-based approaches, recurrent SAC/PPO variants, or task-specific tactile methods are missing.

The ablation study is insufficient for attributing gains. It is unclear how much performance comes from off-policy RL, CrossQ, transformer memory, image encoder design, replay reuse, loss shaping, or hyperparameter tuning.

Some results are only modest over the random baseline, especially TactileMNIST volume estimation, where final errors differ only slightly. This weakens the argument that active policy learning consistently provides large benefits.

The evaluation protocol raises fairness questions: hyperparameters are tuned on selected tasks, APPLE-CrossQ uses one configuration while other methods use different tuned configurations, and HAM is modified from its original reward. More controlled tuning budgets and baseline adaptations would strengthen the comparison.
The method remains very sample- and compute-intensive, requiring millions of simulated interactions and 40-50 hours per 5M-step vision run, which limits practical impact for real tactile robotics.

The paper acknowledges but does not resolve key limitations: scalability to multi-finger hands, real contact dynamics, richer object sets, real-world noise, and broader active perception objectives remain untested.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: learning active perception policies, especially for tactile sensing where observations are sparse and local.
The proposed APPLE formulation is reasonably clear at a high level, combining a sequence model for perception with off-policy RL and a supervised prediction loss.
The evaluation spans several task types, including classification, volume regression, and pose estimation, which is a useful attempt to test generality beyond a single benchmark.
The paper includes random-policy baselines, multiple seeds, appendix details, and hyperparameter tables, which help interpret the empirical results.
Some reported results are promising, especially the improvements over random exploration on TactileMNIST and Toolbox and the apparent robustness of APPLE-CrossQ under reused hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The core method is largely a straightforward combination of transformer sequence modeling, supervised prediction losses, and standard off-policy RL algorithms such as SAC/CrossQ; the paper does not make a compelling case that the formulation is a substantial technical advance.

The experimental evidence is not strong enough for the broad claims of a general active perception framework. All main tactile results are simulated, most tasks come from the same benchmark family, and there is no real-robot validation despite the robotics framing.

The baselines are weak and sometimes poorly matched. The main learned baseline is HAM, which the paper itself notes lacks an image encoder and is unsuitable for several tasks; this makes claims about outperforming the current state of the art unconvincing. More relevant comparisons to modern active perception, information-gain, model-based, PPO/SAC variants, or task-specific heuristics are missing from the main evaluation.

The paper claims task-agnostic generality, but the agents are trained from scratch per task. There is no convincing transfer, multitask training, zero-shot adaptation, or systematic evidence that APPLE learns reusable exploration strategies.

Ablations are insufficient. The paper does not adequately isolate the contribution of the transformer backbone, shared representation, supervised loss gradient, off-policy replay, action regularization, vision encoder, horizon length, or hyperparameter choices.

The gains over random exploration are modest on some regression tasks, particularly TactileMNIST Volume, where improvements are small and variance appears high. This weakens the claim that the method robustly solves diverse active perception problems.

Sample efficiency and practicality are major concerns. The method requires 5M to 10M environment steps and 40-50 GPU hours for some runs, yet sample efficiency is one of the motivations for moving beyond on-policy methods.

The evaluation protocol raises fairness concerns: hyperparameters are tuned on selected tasks and reused elsewhere, but baseline tuning and capacity matching are not clearly sufficient to support strong comparative conclusions.
Reproducibility is only partially addressed. The paper says the codebase will be released, but at submission time the evidence depends on unreleased implementations and simulated environments.

The paper overstates its conclusions, using language such as general, principled, and state-of-the-art without enough breadth of baselines, real-world evidence, or theoretical novelty to support those claims.

strengths: Clear and timely problem formulation: the paper frames active perception as joint policy learning and supervised prediction under a POMDP, which is a useful abstraction for tactile exploration tasks.

The proposed APPLE framework is technically coherent and reasonably simple: augmenting off-policy actor-critic methods with a differentiable prediction loss and a shared transformer backbone is a practical design that can be reused across tasks.

Empirical coverage is broader than many tactile active perception papers, including classification, volume regression, and pose estimation across five benchmarks, with 5 random seeds and both average and final prediction metrics.

The comparisons to HAM and random exploration are informative. In particular, the paper identifies that the original MHSB benchmark can be nearly solved by memorization/random exploration, which is a valuable diagnostic observation.
The appendix provides useful environment, hyperparameter, hardware, and derivation details, and the limitations section is candid about sample inefficiency and the lack of real-world validation.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than exceptional. APPLE is mainly a careful combination of SAC/CrossQ, supervised prediction loss, recurrence/transformer state encoding, and active perception benchmarks; the conceptual ingredients are mostly established.

The central claim of generality is stronger than the evidence. All substantive experiments are simulated tactile settings, mostly from the same benchmark family, with a single-sensor setup; there is no real-robot experiment, multimodal setting, or transfer across substantially different domains.

Baselines are somewhat limited. HAM is an older/on-policy method and cannot handle the visual tactile tasks as implemented; stronger active perception baselines, information-gain/model-based methods, PPO/SAC variants with comparable encoders across all tasks, or non-RL active learning policies would make the evaluation more convincing.

Sample efficiency and compute cost are significant concerns: tactile tasks require 5M-10M simulator steps and around 40-50 GPU-hours per 5M-step run. This weakens the practical robotics relevance unless paired with stronger sim-to-real or pretraining evidence.

Some results are mixed. The volume estimation gains over random are modest, APPLE-SAC performs poorly on Toolbox without tuning, and MHSB is shown to be a weak benchmark because random exploration can solve it.

The reward/action regularization description appears potentially inconsistent: the text calls the action term a penalty but writes it as a positive magnitude term under a maximization objective, which would encourage larger actions unless there is an omitted sign convention.

Reproducibility is promising but not complete in the submitted manuscript: code release is promised rather than provided, and several key outcomes are shown mainly in plots without detailed numerical tables or statistical tests.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: learning active perception policies that jointly gather information and infer task labels/properties under partial observability, with tactile sensing as a well-motivated domain.

The formulation connecting supervised prediction loss with policy optimization is clear and useful, and the APPLE-SAC / APPLE-CrossQ instantiations are natural extensions of strong off-policy RL algorithms.

The experiments cover multiple task types, including classification, volume regression, and pose estimation, and include five seeds, learning curves, random-policy baselines, and several appendix ablations.

The empirical results show meaningful gains over random exploration on several tasks, especially CircleSquare, TactileMNIST, and Toolbox with APPLE-CrossQ, suggesting that learned policies are doing more than passive perception.
The appendix is unusually helpful: it includes environment details, hyperparameter search procedure, additional baselines such as PPO variants, sparse-loss experiments, and implementation details.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. The core idea of combining a supervised prediction objective with an RL policy for active sensing is natural and closely related to RAM/HAM, internally rewarded RL, active vision, and POMDP-based active perception. The paper presents a clean formulation, but the algorithmic contribution is mostly an adaptation of SAC/CrossQ rather than a fundamentally new method.

The evaluation is almost entirely simulated and centered on TactileMNIST-style environments. This weakens the broad claim of a general active perception framework for robotics, especially since no real-robot experiment or realistic sim-to-real validation is provided.

Baselines are limited. HAM is an important comparison but is old, on-policy, and lacks the image encoder needed for key tasks. Stronger comparisons are missing, such as recurrent SAC/CrossQ without the proposed supervised-gradient coupling, active inference/information-gain heuristics, learned next-best-view baselines, scripted search policies for tactile tasks, or oracle/upper-bound exploration strategies.

Some reported improvements are modest or mixed. On TactileMNISTVolume the learned policies only slightly improve over random exploration, and APPLE-SAC fails badly on Toolbox without retuning. This makes the robustness and generality claims stronger than the evidence supports.

The task design sometimes favors the proposed setup. CircleSquare includes a background gradient that effectively provides directional guidance, and the MHSB task is shown to be solvable by memorization/random touches. These are useful diagnostics but not very convincing as evidence of general active perception.

The reward/action regularization description appears inconsistent: the text calls r(ht, at)=10^-3||at||^2 a regularizing penalty, but under reward maximization this is positive and would encourage larger actions unless a negative sign is intended. This should be clarified because it affects reproducibility and interpretation.

Reproducibility is incomplete for a top-tier submission. The paper gives many implementation details but does not clearly state that code, environments, trained models, or exact benchmark splits will be released; reproducing 40-50 hour GPU runs with large hyperparameter searches would be difficult.

Theoretical treatment is mostly motivational. The derivation explains the gradient decomposition, but the off-policy training with a nonstationary learned prediction loss/reward is not analyzed, and stability issues from recomputing rewards with evolving predictors are not deeply discussed.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant active perception problem and formulates perception as an interactive supervised-learning/POMDP objective, which is a reasonable unifying perspective for classification and regression settings.
The architecture and training recipe are clearly motivated: a shared transformer backbone supports sequence integration, while SAC/CrossQ provide off-policy sample reuse for active data gathering.

The empirical section covers several simulated tasks, including classification, volume regression, and pose estimation, and includes some useful ablations against random policies, PPO/HAM variants, LSTM backbones, pure-RL prediction, grid search, sparse loss, and longer HAM runs.
The results do show that learned active policies can outperform random exploration on several tasks, especially CircleSquare, TactileMNIST classification, and Toolbox with APPLE-CrossQ.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The central algorithm is largely a combination of standard supervised prediction loss with standard off-policy actor-critic methods and a transformer sequence encoder. The paper does not make a compelling case that this is a substantially new algorithmic contribution rather than an application/engineering recipe.

The main claims about a general active perception framework are much stronger than the evidence. All main results are in simulation, mostly tactile-style toy or benchmark settings, with no real-robot validation and no demonstration on materially different sensing modalities or downstream robotic tasks.

The baseline set is weak. The strongest comparisons are random exploration, HAM, and PPO-style variants. There is little comparison to task-specific active perception methods, information-gain methods, active sensing heuristics, model-based approaches, or stronger modern recurrent/off-policy RL baselines. This makes it hard to judge significance.

Some performance gains are modest. On TactileMNISTVolume, final error improves only slightly over random exploration, and on CIFAR10 the gap over random is also limited. APPLE-SAC fails or underperforms in Toolbox, leaving robustness claims mainly dependent on APPLE-CrossQ.

The evaluation is very sample intensive, requiring millions to ten million environment steps and long GPU runs. This weakens the practicality of the method, especially for tactile robotics where real-world interaction is expensive.

The paper’s strongest negative claims about HAM/on-policy methods are not fully justified. HAM lacks the same image encoder and architecture, and failures on CircleSquare may reflect architecture and tuning choices as much as an inherent limitation of on-policy active perception.

Reproducibility is incomplete for a top-tier submission. Hyperparameters and hardware are reported, but I do not see a clear code/data release statement, full training protocol details sufficient for independent reproduction, or a careful accounting of hyperparameter search budget across methods.

Theoretical contribution is thin. The derivation mostly decomposes the gradient into policy-gradient and supervised-loss terms under standard assumptions, but it does not provide new guarantees, convergence analysis, or a deeper treatment of nonstationarity from jointly learned perception rewards.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: learning active perception policies that can gather sparse local information, especially in tactile settings where purposeful exploration is essential.

The formulation of active perception as an interactive supervised learning problem embedded in a POMDP is clean and useful. The combination of RL policy learning with direct supervised prediction-loss gradients is intuitive and broadly applicable across classification and regression objectives.

The proposed APPLE-SAC and APPLE-CrossQ instantiations are technically plausible and well matched to the problem. The shared transformer-based temporal representation for perception, policy, and critic is a sensible architectural choice for sequential tactile observations.

The empirical evaluation is broader than many active tactile perception papers: it covers toy visual search, tactile MNIST classification, tactile volume estimation, toolbox pose estimation, MHSB comparison, and an appendix CIFAR-10 glimpse task, with five seeds and held-out objects/images where applicable.

The results convincingly show that learned active policies outperform random exploration on several tasks, with especially strong evidence on CircleSquare, TactileMNIST classification, and Toolbox using APPLE-CrossQ.

The paper includes useful ablations and supplementary analyses, including pure-RL prediction variants, grid-search comparison, sparse reward variants, longer HAM validation, hyperparameter search details, implementation notes, and limitations.

The authors are appropriately transparent about sample inefficiency and simulation-only evaluation, and the learned behavior visualizations help support the claim that the policies are doing meaningful information gathering rather than only exploiting dataset artifacts.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than high. The main algorithmic contribution is largely an integration of existing off-policy RL methods, supervised prediction losses, and transformer sequence models for active perception; the conceptual framing is useful, but not a major technical breakthrough.

The baseline set is too limited for the strength of the generality claims. The main comparisons are random exploration and HAM, with HAM being an older on-policy method that lacks an image encoder and is not a strong modern baseline for most evaluated tasks. More competitive baselines such as PPO/SAC variants with different architectures, information-gain or uncertainty-driven policies, heuristic search policies for tactile tasks, and task-specific active perception methods would make the evidence much stronger.

Several headline gains are task-dependent or modest. On TactileMNIST-Volume, final error improves only slightly over random exploration, and APPLE-SAC fails to learn a strong policy on Toolbox without tuning. This weakens the claim that the framework robustly handles diverse regression active perception problems.

The evaluation is entirely simulated and relies heavily on the TactileMNIST benchmark suite. This is reasonable for a first study, but the paper’s robotics motivation would be better supported by real tactile experiments or at least stronger sim-to-real discussion with empirical evidence.

The method is very sample- and compute-intensive, requiring up to 5M-10M environment steps and 40-50 hours per vision-based run on a high-end GPU. This limits practical applicability, especially for real robotic active tactile perception.

The generality claim is somewhat overstated. The tasks share similar low-dimensional continuous movement actions and mostly single-sensor tactile/visual-glimpse structure; it remains unclear how well APPLE scales to multi-finger hands, multimodal sensing, higher-dimensional manipulation actions, or downstream control tasks where perception is only an intermediate requirement.

The theoretical derivation mainly motivates adding supervised loss gradients to policy-gradient learning, but it does not provide strong guarantees or a careful treatment of practical off-policy approximations, shared-representation interference, or stability issues that may arise from jointly optimizing prediction and control objectives.

Reproducibility details are fairly good, but the paper does not clearly state whether code, trained models, and benchmark configurations will be released. Given the high compute cost and several implementation-sensitive choices, this matters for independent verification.
